subject: Computer Networking
title: MQTT: Messaging for IoT
description: A 60-second lesson on MQTT: Messaging for IoT.

hook.text: A tiny sensor on a farm sends temperature readings every minute. It has almost no bandwidth. MQTT is perfect.

buildup.text: MQTT is a lightweight publish-subscribe messaging protocol designed for constrained devices and unreliable networks.

discovery.text: Devices publish to topics. Subscribers get messages from topics they follow. Efficient and fully decoupled.

twist.text: MQTT's overhead is as small as 2 bytes per message. Compare that to HTTP's hundreds of header bytes.

climax.text: Smart homes, factory sensors, fleet tracking — billions of IoT devices rely on MQTT for lightweight communication.

punchline.text: MQTT sends tiny messages from tiny devices. Big impact.

quiz.question: Why is MQTT ideal for IoT devices?
options: Its minimal overhead works on constrained devices and networks
It provides the fastest file transfers available
It replaces TCP for all internet traffic

details.summary: MQTT is a lightweight publish-subscribe messaging protocol designed for constrained devices and unreliable networks. Clients publish messages to topics and subscribe to receive messages from topics, with a broker handling all routing. Three QoS levels balance reliability against bandwidth.
details.whyItMatters: MQTT is the dominant protocol for IoT communication, connecting billions of sensors and devices. Its minimal overhead makes it work on devices with limited processing power and bandwidth.
takeaways: Publish-subscribe model decouples message senders from receivers
Three QoS levels offer at-most-once to exactly-once delivery
Minimal protocol overhead suits constrained IoT devices

faq.question: How does MQTT's publish-subscribe model work?
faq.answer: Devices publish messages to named topics through a central broker. Other devices subscribe to topics they care about. The broker routes messages from publishers to all matching subscribers. This decoupling means publishers and subscribers do not need to know about each other.

faq.question: What are MQTT QoS levels?
faq.answer: QoS 0 delivers messages at most once with no confirmation. QoS 1 ensures at-least-once delivery with acknowledgment but may duplicate. QoS 2 guarantees exactly-once delivery using a four-step handshake. Higher QoS uses more bandwidth, so IoT devices often use QoS 0 or 1.
